records.title: Content moderation and personal visibility controls
facts: Authenticated users can use the final Flag Content entry in a Wave post's More menu on desktop or action sheet on mobile to report, hide, block, or combine those actions.
No action is selected by default. Reporting automatically hides the post for the reporter; hide-only and block-only actions remain available, and blocking is still optional when reporting.

Only the reporter sees the compact Reported or Reviewed control inside the post. It opens report details and keeps the submitted Report option checked and locked; Reveal is temporary, Unhide removes only the personal hide, and neither withdraws the report.

An open report can be withdrawn from a separate confirmation state until a moderator resolves it. A successful withdrawal closes the dialog, leaves the post hidden, does not affect other reporters, and permits that profile to report the post later. After either reviewed outcome, the same profile cannot report the unchanged post again, while other profiles may still report it independently.
Reporters see only Awaiting review, No action taken, or Content removed outcomes; moderator identity, internal notes, AI details, and other reporters remain private.

Personally hidden posts and posts from blocked authors keep their original layout under a non-interactive blur. Reveal is temporary; Unhide and Unblock persist through the API and update mounted posts immediately.

Notification, messaging, blocked-profile, and report-history settings are combined at /preferences. Blocked Profiles is available at /preferences?tab=blocked-profiles, Reports is available at /preferences?tab=reports, and the older content-preferences paths resolve to Blocked Profiles.

The Reports tab lists reports submitted by the current profile, a snapshot of each reported post, its Wave name and picture, and its public review status. The Wave remains linked after removal; visible posts also link to their exact Wave or direct-message context, while media and files stay collapsed by default. Open reports can be withdrawn there; AI assessments, parent evidence, internal notes or reasons, moderator identity, and other reporters are not exposed.
Preferences are profile-scoped. An authenticated wallet without a profile sees a Create profile action instead of a connection prompt, and the controls become available after profile creation.

A blocked profile's avatar and handle in Preferences link to its public profile. Its profile header shows a red-tinted Blocked status beside the handle, keeps Direct Message available, and puts a separate confirmation-backed Unblock action where Follow normally appears.

Blocking hides the profile's content, treats its activity as muted, automatically unfollows it, and prevents following again until it is unblocked. It does not notify the blocked profile or remove that profile's subscription to the blocker.

Unblocked profile headers place icon-labelled Mute notifications or Unmute notifications and Block profile in one responsive profile-actions menu instead of showing a standalone mute button. Desktop uses an overflow menu, while mobile browsers and the mobile app use a bottom sheet. Blocking still requires confirmation.

Blocked public profiles remain reachable. Public profile and Brain summary metadata stays visible, while each Brain activity post keeps its normal height under a blur with visible Wave information. Reveal is temporary and changes to Hide again without resizing the card.

Blocking does not prevent one-to-one direct-message creation or delivery. The blocker's existing and future conversation is instead treated as muted and deprioritized, blocked-author messages stay hidden until individually revealed, and the other profile receives no block disclosure.

Group direct messages and shared Waves remain usable and are not muted as a whole. Blocked-author posts stay hidden and do not create ordinary notifications, push notifications, or direct-message unread counts for the blocker; other members behave normally.

Globally quarantined or moderator-removed posts cannot be revealed. Primary Wave chat keeps author, time, and Wave context while replacing only the body; compact secondary surfaces use a redacted tombstone.
The author can still see their own globally moderated post and its moderation state; other viewers receive redacted content.

Only server-authorized moderators see and can use the WatchTower side-navigation item at /content-moderation on desktop, mobile browser, and mobile app. It is not in the profile menu. The page heading is WatchTower - Content Moderation.

WatchTower identifies both the author and reporter, separates Open reports, Resolved reports, Suspended profiles, and Block activity, and lets moderators select one explained content decision, optionally add an internal note, and apply it once. All tabs share the standard bordered page frame.

WatchTower tabs have direct URLs: /content-moderation/open-reports, /content-moderation/resolved-reports, /content-moderation/suspended-profiles, and /content-moderation/block-activity. Switching tabs updates the URL without reloading the page. Direct links and refresh open the selected tab, browser Back and Forward restore tab selections, and /content-moderation defaults to Open reports. Moderator authorization applies to every tab URL.

Block activity is a newest-first, continuously loaded moderator trail showing who blocked or unblocked whom in the same feed. Aligned rows link both available profiles without truncating handles and show the event date. Blocked uses red text and a closed lock; Unblocked uses green text and an open lock. Only actual relationship transitions are recorded; unblocking preserves the earlier block in history. The feed remains independent from reports, AI assessment, content decisions, and suspension.
Allow keeps or restores a post to visible and closes its reports; Quarantine hides it globally while reports remain open; Remove hides it globally and closes its reports as removed.

Profile suspension is separate from the post decision, prevents future creates and edits without changing existing posts, and can be reversed from the central Suspended profiles view or a moderator-only profile action. A moderator's personal Blocked state remains independent.
WatchTower omits the neutral AI category NONE and labels a substantive AI result as a Potential category because the moderator decision remains authoritative.

A still-valid saved session can authorize posting and other authenticated actions without an active wallet connection or supported signing network. If the session expires, the app preserves the connection and profile selection, checks that signing is available before invalidating the expired session, and requests a new signature only when it can safely continue.
WatchTower shows a red navigation indicator while open reports need review and refreshes that lightweight state periodically while the app is active.
Someone who opens /content-moderation without moderator access sees a countdown and is redirected home; a failed access check shows an error instead of being treated as a denial.

records.title: Pre-publication safety check
aliases: can I swear in a post
facts: New and edited Wave posts receive a narrow server-side safety check before the backend writes them; this includes chat messages, replies, and direct messages because they are stored as drops.

Most posts pass a lightweight deterministic screen without an AI call. Only a specific risk signal is escalated to a permissive AI check, and rejection requires a high-confidence prohibited-content result.
Profanity, unpopular opinions, and ordinary offensive speech are not rejected merely for being objectionable.
Configured known unsafe destinations can be rejected directly. Uncertain AI results and evaluator failures follow the permissive policy and allow the post.

Structured private-data patterns, including US Social Security number patterns and Luhn-valid payment-card candidates, are sent to the AI check. Clearly labelled fictitious, sandbox, test, example, redacted, or documentation data is allowed, while a genuine usable private identifier can be rejected whether it belongs to the author or another person; ownership claims and known test status are context rather than automatic allow rules.
A locally created post stays visible in its normal layout while submission is pending; it is not replaced by a prominent checking message.

When the backend rejects a post, the unsent optimistic post remains temporarily in the current Wave with a subtle red treatment and a 'Not sent · Blocked by safety check' status; it is never persisted and disappears after leaving or refreshing the Wave.
A moderation-rejected local row does not offer edit, retry, reaction, reply, or post-action controls.
File attachments such as PDF and CSV files use a separate asynchronous validation pipeline rather than the synchronous text check.

records.title: Posting suspension
aliases: why can't I edit my post
facts: Posting suspension is applied manually by an authorized moderator; a report or AI result does not suspend a profile automatically.
A suspended profile cannot publish new or edited drop content, including chat messages, replies, and direct messages.
Posting suspension does not sign the user out, stop them reading the site, delete existing posts, or hide existing posts.
A posting suspension has no automatic expiry and remains in place until an authorized moderator reinstates the profile.
A rejected posting attempt directs the user to contact support if they believe the suspension is a mistake.

records.title: 6529 Network Museum
facts: The 6529 Network Museum presents itself at /museum/network as the public art museum of the 6529 Network: a permanent digital-art collection held by the Network on Ethereum, governed through TDH, and open worldwide.

The homepage establishes one institutional proposition and introduces the Casey Reas, Keys and Gates, and Magnum Photos 75 acquisition stories through artwork-led presentations. The Collection page contains twelve accessioned works: seven by Casey Reas and five from Magnum Photos 75.

The complete institutional proposition is at /museum/network/about. It explains what Network holding means, the absence of fractional or economic claims for members, the Museum's present delegated operating boundaries, the on-chain direction, and the permanence objective.
Keys and Gates is published at /museum/network/acquisition-programs/keys-and-gates with sixteen selected photographs and its program record.
The sixteen Keys and Gates works carry the status Selected through the Keys and Gates program; minting and acquisition will follow, and the permanent Collection begins at formal accession.

Keys and Gates presents all sixteen selected works through reviewed Museum-hosted display surrogates with source, fixity, rights, credit, and accessibility records. Selection, minting, acquisition, and accession remain independent facts.
Collection means works formally accessioned by the Museum at /museum/network/collection; canonical Work records are available at /museum/network/works/[work-id].
Artists, projects, organizations, acquisitions, and research connect works to curatorial writing, provenance, rights, and collection care.
Acquisitions at /museum/network/acquisitions presents Casey Reas, Keys and Gates, and Magnum Photos 75 with each present stage and its related works.
Magnum Photos 75, Conflict at Its Edges, is an accessioned gift of five photographs in the permanent Collection at /museum/network/acquisitions/conflict-at-its-edges.
The Museum adapter resolves canonical 6529-Collections/6529networkmuseum main to one exact commit, validates the release inventory, and activates the complete public publication atomically.
The governed Gift into Public Trust narrative and all five Casey Reas project essays are readable onsite from the same atomic publication snapshot.
Inside the System publishes project-level studies for CENTURY, Pre-Process, Phototaxis, 923 EMPTY ROOMS, and Ex Nihilo (Cosmos) at /museum/network/projects/[project-slug]/system.
Each study keeps the Museum artwork fixed and lets visitors compare any minted work by edition number, token ID, random selection, or published-trait filter.
Try a variation changes selected conditions in a clearly labeled Museum model. It does not generate or claim a new Casey Reas artwork.
Copy comparison link preserves the selected work and the complete versioned Museum-model or restaged-session settings, so the same view opens after reload.

Suggested comparisons use published traits and the Museum's reviewed NextGen-compatible descriptor for the pinned edition snapshot. They are not judgments of quality or value and use no marketplace data.
Every project also provides a visual map and semantic data table, traces the causal algorithm, and locates the Museum's held works without ranking quality, price, or desirability.
Generative studies belong to projects rather than gifts, so later accessions from the same project can be added to the same analysis.
Research is published at /museum/network/research, with sources and chronology, art and artists, Museum practice, and sources and methods available as distinct reading paths.

A field of practice is published at /museum/network/stories/a-field-of-practice with a comparative essay, twenty-seven institutional profiles, an adjacent-practice study, the public scholarship and editorial standard, and a primary-source register admitted from one exact Museum source release.

The System in Seven States and Conflict at Its Edges are formally accessioned gifts in the permanent Collection. Keys and Gates carries the selected-program status; its works remain unminted and outside the Collection.

Official Art Blocks still and live URLs remain labeled upstream presentation sources for Casey Reas. Keys and Gates uses reviewed Museum-hosted display surrogates; Conflict at Its Edges uses reviewed signed-Wave display sources.
The public release supplies current status. Accession, rights, ownership, and preservation records each carry their own evidence.
The Museum repository is the transitional public working record: visitors can inspect exact source commits, fork the repository, and propose reviewed changes through pull requests.

Every Museum page carries a quiet source and contribution strip. Exact inspection links stay bound to the verified release commit; the actionable contributor guide points to canonical main so its instructions remain current.
The Open Museum operating statement is working public guidance with policy adoption pending. The on-chain transition statement is a working migration statement awaiting deployment evidence.

The Museum has an accessioned collection, adopted collecting policies, TDH-weighted decisions, dedicated Ethereum custody, and a public machine-readable record. Current operations use public repository records and Museum Safe signers.
The planned on-chain system is designed to connect independently verifiable decisions, decision-constrained custody, and execution. Deployment and activation remain future steps.

The permanence objective requires Ethereum state, content-addressed records, preserved media and software, rights and provenance evidence, migration paths, and replaceable interfaces. Preservation is a documented institutional practice.

The study is at /museum/network/stories/a-field-of-practice; each institution has its own profile, adjacent chain-native practice is at /museum/network/stories/a-field-of-practice/adjacent-practice, the public writing standard is at /museum/network/stories/scholarship-and-writing, and the primary-source register is at /museum/network/stories/a-field-of-practice/sources.

The twenty-seven profiles are organized into four reading paths: software, networks, and technical culture; media art across regions; collection and conservation; and scholarship, archives, and long duration.
Each profile presents demonstrated practices, what the Network Museum should adopt, the limits of the comparison, and its sources.
The study is a research instrument rather than a ranking; the profiles keep lessons and analytical limits attached to their institutional context.

The comparative essay, all twenty-seven profiles, the adjacent-practice study, the scholarship and editorial standard, and the source register must validate from the same exact Museum repository commit before the site publishes the study.
Read the source opens the immutable manuscript used for the page. Propose an edit opens the maintained manuscript on main, and Contributor guide explains the reviewed pull-request process.
The source register records each primary source, its displayed date, its source type, and the evidence drawn from it.
If the current source cannot be verified, the Museum may serve a clearly identified last complete release; it never combines manuscripts from different source releases.

Its existing section anchors remain stable, and archived version routes keep their exact editorial snapshot.

It separates pinned contract behavior, accepted ADR design, and the still-proposed ERC-20 path. Archived version routes keep their exact editorial snapshot.

The current Randomness page starts with a one-minute answer and a five-step request flow. It separates reviewed code from accepted ADR 0005 design and open recovery ideas, then explains provider trust, request states, seed evidence, same-seed retries, stale requests, provider changes, burns, funding, risks, and reviewer questions. Archived version routes keep their exact editorial snapshot.

The current For Artists page begins with a plain artist guide covering the artwork plan, its lifecycle, approval, roles, sales, changes, and permanence. It then replaces the archived technical text with fifteen short sections. The sections use Reviewed code, Accepted design, and Still proposed labels. They cover identity, artist approval, records, artwork files, editions, minting, curation, sales, revenue, randomness, freezing, lifetime authority, design goals, and artist questions. Archived version routes keep their exact editorial snapshot.

The current Who Can Do What page replaces the archived technical text with a plain status-first guide. It separates powers working in the current rehearsal, connected for integration, built in source, planned, and still open. It also explains duties outside the contracts, main risks, and reviewer questions. Archived version routes keep their exact editorial snapshot.

The current Changes, Emergencies, and Future Contracts page starts with a short explanation of setup sealing, delayed changes, pauses, permanent powers, and replacement contracts. It separates current code, accepted ADR 0017, open governance risks, and launch evidence. It also explains that the 30-day successor class and 48-hour module registration are separate in the pinned source. Archived version routes keep their exact editorial snapshot.

The current Metadata, Scripts, and Dependencies page begins with a one-minute explanation. It separates behavior in the pinned Solidity, accepted design in ADR 0006, unbuilt satellite refresh helpers, and external compatibility evidence. It keeps detailed source links, risks, and reviewer questions, while archived version routes keep their exact editorial snapshot.

The current Where Development Stands page begins by answering whether Stream is ready to launch. It says not yet, lists the three remaining launch gates in plain language, and shows the last checked date plus the open release-blocker count. The next sections explain what the review covers, use five plain progress labels, and explain what each kind of proof shows and does not show. Built code stays separate from safety evidence, accepted plans stay separate from unaccepted designs, and ADRs are not treated as implementation or launch proof. The exact commit and Git tree follow under Technical details.
The current Community Review page begins with six focused review questions and the review authorship disclosure.

Fourteen editorial pages explain artwork lifecycle, artist controls, responsibilities, curation and TDH authorization, minting, sales, revenue, randomness, metadata, freezing, contract changes, current development, and community review.

Current review pages show lifecycle, deployment, and audit status plus an exact source link, page navigation, and a collapsible feedback rail without exposing an archive version number. Saved snapshot pages show their exact review version and link back to the current review. Detailed editorial pages also show on-page contents, while the simplified current Overview omits hidden technical headings. Snapshot evidence is collected on Where Development Stands.

Review chapters stay in the review contents navigation. Technical reference, All public feedback, and Review history are separate review-wide destinations on current pages; Review history opens the immutable technical Overview for the active snapshot. Page comments and sending feedback remain page-specific actions.
Active and historical routes read immutable versioned editorial content and validate its manifest before rendering.

Each immutable version has its own lifecycle, deployment status, and audit status: superseded versions can remain readable as REVIEW_CLOSED, stop accepting submissions, link back to the current review, and avoid inheriting newer deployment or audit claims.
The generated technical reference exposes the exact versioned Solidity source, definitions, functions, events, errors, and other declarations.

The all-declarations explorer applies its text, kind, scope, and location filters on the server and returns at most 100 matches per page instead of sending the complete declaration inventory to the browser.

Every editorial page combines its version-scoped comments and structured feedback composer in a collapsible rail that docks beside wide documents and opens as a dismissible right-side overlay on narrower layouts.
The reusable lifecycle map supports draft, scheduled, public review, review closed, remediation, audit, final candidate, deployed, and archived states; only public review accepts new feedback.

records.title: Stream review feedback and public ledger
facts: Every Stream editorial and technical reference page has one structured feedback composer connected to the server-resolved Stream review Wave destination.

Editorial pages place the current page's loaded comments and composer in one collapsible rail; closing and reopening it preserves the current draft, and the browser remembers the open or closed preference.
The page-comments rail reads the most recent 50 Wave messages for the exact review version, shows entries attached to the current page, and can load older 50-message pages on request.
Editorial feedback can reference a stable page section; technical feedback can reference an exact Solidity file and line range.
A code-reference submission remains unavailable until the browser computes the exact selected snippet checksum; changing the selection invalidates any earlier preview but preserves the written draft.

If a reviewer edits the draft or changes its attached page, section, or source range while a post is in flight, a successful response preserves the newer work and the next post uses a fresh submission ID.
A successful feedback post uses the standard app toast; Open discussion in the Wave remains the single route from the review back to the posted discussion.
Every submission carries the immutable review version, page or section, category, suspected severity, and exact source provenance when code is selected.
Possible exploitable security vulnerabilities are intentionally submitted to the same public review during Stream's predeployment lifecycle.

The review records a source-confirmed limitation in which finalizing an unfrozen collection before any token is minted writes zero, which setCollectionData can later treat as uninitialized and replace with a nonzero cap; the candidate needs a monotonic finalization guard or equivalent before this promise is irreversible.
Public vulnerability submission is available only during the PUBLIC_REVIEW lifecycle state; deployed reviews use their configured post-deployment disclosure policy.
The public feedback ledger supports category, page, contract, severity, disposition, and text filters plus CSV and Markdown auditor exports.
Ledger entries are identified and deduplicated by immutable Wave drop ID rather than the client-supplied submission UUID.
Ledger metadata for a 50-drop page is hydrated in batches of no more than eight concurrent requests.
A feedback section is accepted only when that exact section is explicitly allowed for the selected page; pages without a section allow-list accept no section IDs.

Immutable review-version routes have their own version-filtered feedback ledger and exact source-commit banner; review versions 2026-07-26.1, 2026-07-27.1, and 2026-07-30.1 are retained with feedback closed while 2026-08-01.1 is the active writing revision.

The current Community Review page includes the visible authorship note explaining that bots wrote the review under punk6529's mission and standards; immutable versioned editorial pages retain the disclosure used by their snapshot routes.
Ledger code links open the immutable in-site versioned source and also provide the pinned GitHub source.

records.title: 6529 FAQ
facts: The 6529 FAQ lives at /about/faq.
6529 and 6529.io refer to the same product ecosystem in user questions.
6529 is building a decentralized network state: a permissionless global network society that funds, builds, and coordinates public-goods work across art, science, culture, and technology.

In product terms, 6529 is not only an NFT collection site; it is a coordination system built around wallet identity, profiles, The Memes, Meme Lab, Gradients, NextGen, Waves, voting, groups, delegation, REP/CIC reputation, TDH/xTDH network metrics, open data, minting/claims infrastructure, and help tooling such as @help6529.
The long-term goal is nation-scale positive impact.

The core idea is to extend what Bitcoin and Ethereum proved for money and code into human coordination itself, so communities can organize, allocate attention, vote, build, and distribute work permissionlessly.

records.title: TDH
facts: TDH means Total Days Held.
TDH does not stand for Total Dynamic Head.
TDH is 6529's time-weighted holding metric for eligible NFTs.
Conceptually, TDH measures long-term participation and skin in the 6529 ecosystem.
Each eligible NFT contributes value based on how long it has been held; that base holding time is then adjusted by edition-size weighting and by collection boosters.
The calculation has three layers: unweighted days, edition weighting, and boosts.
Unweighted days means each NFT contributes 1 unit per day it is held.
Edition weighting means days held are multiplied by a HODL or edition-size rate; on the frontend TDH page, FirstGM with edition size 3,941 is the 1.0 baseline.
Boosts multiply weighted TDH by active boosters based on what the holder owns.

The backend stores the distinctions separately: tdh__raw is raw full days held, tdh is raw days multiplied by HODL or edition weighting, and boosted_tdh is weighted TDH multiplied by the active boost.
Current TDH 1.4 rules use the higher of Category A or Category B boosters, plus Category C.
Category A is the complete Meme Card set boost, with diminishing additional-set boosts.
Category B covers season, genesis, and nakamoto set boosts.
Category C is the Gradient boost, up to 5 Gradients.
The current TDH guide presents the Category A or Category B comparison before Category C, then groups formulas, examples, season boosts, limits, and related destinations for quick reference.
TDH is calculated daily at 00:00 UTC and is used throughout the network: profiles, leaderboards, Levels, groups, Network views, Waves voting and eligibility, and public data.

facts: TDH (unboosted) is TDH weighted by edition size before boosters are applied.

The current Nakamoto Set boost shown on the TDH page is 1.01x.

records.title: Network Levels
facts: Network Levels are an integrated signal based on TDH and REP.
The levels page presents its explanation above a full-width table of all Level 0 through 100 thresholds.
When a signed-in active profile is available, the levels page shows its current Level, combined TDH and REP, next Level, and additional amount needed; an active proxy profile takes precedence.
Signed-out users and users whose profile data is unavailable see the general reference page without a personalized empty state or calculator.
Levels are shown across profile and Network surfaces where relevant.

records.title: xTDH Overview
facts: xTDH is an extension of TDH that lets TDH-like network participation flow beyond core 6529 holders to other NFT holders and communities.
xTDH can be earned by holding eligible cards outside The Memes ecosystem.
The frontend /network/xtdh page is labeled xTDH Overview and describes xTDH as an extension of TDH that helps include other NFT holders in the 6529 ecosystem and offer them the benefits of TDH.
xTDH tracks how much xTDH your Memes produce, how much xTDH you receive from grants on tokens you own, and how much xTDH you have granted away.
Produced xTDH comes from TDH production: produced_xTDH_today = TDH gained today * xTDH_coefficient.
The current backend coefficient is 0.1.
Daily xTDH rate is xtdh_rate = produced_today - granted_out_today + received_today.
Total xTDH accumulates as xtdh_total = xtdh_total_previous + xtdh_rate.
The key idea is grants: a profile that produces xTDH can grant future xTDH flow to all tokens in an external ERC-721 collection or to a selected subset of tokens.
If you own a token with an active grant, you receive your share of that grant while you own the token.

Per-token grant flow is grant_amount_per_token = rate / denominator, where the denominator is either the collection total supply for full-collection grants or the number of selected tokens for partial grants.
Transfers inside the same consolidation group do not reset the ownership window; sales or transfers across groups do reset it.
The first grant increment requires the grant and token ownership to have matured past the required midnight or 24-hour windows.

xTDH is not simply TDH for external NFTs; it is a grant and allocation layer where TDH producers create xTDH, can grant future production outward, external token owners can receive it, and ungranted or ineligible flow remains with the grantor.
No produced xTDH is intended to disappear; it is allocated to someone.
For live network-wide xTDH allocation data, use the xTDH Allocations Dashboard at /xtdh.
Profile xTDH information is available under /{user}/xtdh when visible.

CIC is the community interaction count signal shown on profiles and Network surfaces.
REP category analytics and category-level views live under /rep/categories.

records.title: Waves
facts: Waves are the main social threads for conversations, drops, reactions, voting, and wave-specific activity.
Standard wave threads live at /waves/{waveId}; direct messages live at /messages/{waveId}.
Public wave content can remain readable for authenticated wallets without a profile, but posting and other participation actions require profile setup.
The Waves panel includes wave lists, pinned waves, highly rated waves, a Discover Waves link, and create controls.
In Worth Checking Out, each avatar and its overlaid score shield form one wave navigation link; hovering or focusing the combined link shows score details.
Every Worth Checking Out recommendation also appears in All at its recent-activity position; Joined includes only waves the user has joined.

records.title: Drop
facts: A drop is a message posted in a wave.
Drops are written with the wave composer and can include text, markdown, mentions, emoji shortcodes, image uploads, and NFT hashtag references.
Depending on the wave type and rules, other members can react to, vote on, quote, reply to, boost, or pin drops.
Standard wave threads live at /waves/{waveId}; direct-message drops live at /messages/{waveId}.

records.title: Summary proposal cards
facts: The 6529 Network Museum Wave predates proposal-card recipe metadata, so it uses a compatibility fallback: Summary card with 360 characters and the first ready still image enabled. A Wave admin can replace that fallback from Settings, and the saved choice takes precedence.
Other existing standard Waves keep their current presentation unless the Wave is explicitly configured to use custom proposal cards.

A compact card uses the proposal's stored title or first authored non-empty line, an excerpt from the original authored text, real multipart/media/attachment counts, and at most one ready static image preview.
Compact proposal cards do not generate summaries, categories, or proposal metadata.
Selecting a proposal card opens the complete original proposal, including its full markdown, media, attachments, and multipart navigation.
Memes, Curation, and Quorum Waves keep their specialized proposal presentations.

Wave creators can choose Full proposal or Summary card under Advanced settings in the Overview step for a Rank or Approve Wave. New Waves default to Summary card; existing Waves and older drafts without this setting keep Full proposal except for the Network Museum compatibility fallback.

Wave admins can change the same presentation later from the right sidebar under Settings, Display, Proposal cards. This control is available for standard Rank and Approve Waves, not Chat, Memes, Curation, or Quorum presentations.

Summary card lets the admin set a proposal-text limit from 120 to 1000 characters and choose whether the first ready still image appears beside proposal summaries in chat and list views. Invalid limits cannot be saved. Full proposal media is unchanged.

records.title: Parent wave unread subwave count
facts: The new badge beside a parent wave's subwave control totals unread drops across visible, unmuted subwaves where read state is available.
A subwave contributes to the parent badge whether or not the viewer has joined or followed it.
The total excludes the viewer's own drops and drops from muted profiles; muting the parent hides the aggregate.

records.title: Create a subwave
facts: Eligible admins can open the + menu in a root wave's tab row and select New subwave on web or in the app.
New subwave is hidden in direct messages, inside an existing subwave, while using a profile proxy, when the parent has no reusable admin group, or when the profile cannot administer the parent.
A new subwave starts with the parent wave's admin group, and the creator can choose a different existing admin group in the Groups step before submitting.

records.title: Create a wave from the Waves panel
facts: To create a wave on web, click the + button in the Waves panel or open /waves?create=wave.
If the connected identity has no profile handle, Create Wave opens a Create your profile first dialog with Go to Identity and Not now instead of opening the multi-step form.
With a profile handle, Create Wave opens in a centered modal on desktop and the standard bottom sheet below 768px; both use the same multi-step form.
The app full-page create route remains /waves/create where app mode uses it.
Wave creation requires a connected profile and the necessary permissions for the selected groups/settings.

records.title: Wave creation flow
facts: The wave creation flow starts with Overview and then configures groups, description, and additional steps depending on wave type.

The Overview step begins with the Create Wave heading and keeps the wave name, picture, type, and Rank ranking mode visible; Appearance and labels contains display, proposal-card, and applicable tab-label customization.
Optional sections are named for their contents instead of repeating Advanced settings. They show Customized for non-default values and open automatically when a hidden field needs attention.
The Groups step shows all access and moderation rows immediately, organized from Visibility through Admins without an Advanced settings disclosure.
In Groups, Visibility controls wave access; followers who can view the wave may get a notification when it is created.

Each Groups access row offers Edit criteria and Choose group; Edit criteria keeps Identities alongside the rule choices, supports explicitly included and excluded identities, and Next stays disabled until the pending replacement is created, discarded, or replaced by a saved group.

The inline criteria editor includes a Hide criteria and members switch. Its tooltip explains that the criteria and member list remain visible to group members but are hidden from everyone else. The switch starts off for a new inline group, preserves the setting copied from a selected saved group, and applies the current setting when Create and use new group is selected.

The inline Identities editor can add either included or excluded identities through profile search, an authenticated EMMA allowlist, or a dragged or selected CSV file. Source wallets are normalized and deduplicated, source choices persist while the group remains an unsaved draft, and the latest include or exclude action wins when the same wallet appears on both sides.
Inline group identity search ranks exact, prefix, and substring profile-handle matches before ENS-only matches, then orders each match group by profile level, highest first.
An empty Visibility, drop, vote, or chat scope is labeled Public without a Current group heading; after a group is selected, the heading and its current eligible identity count are shown.
A selected saved access group shows its current eligible identity count; View members opens a paginated, searchable member browser without leaving wave creation.
A valid unsaved inline group offers Preview matches, which evaluates current membership without saving the group or applying it to the Wave.
Group membership previews use current profile, reputation, and ownership data, so the matching identities can change over time.

If an older saved draft references a group whose criteria are unavailable, the member browser explains that limitation and continues showing any current members it can resolve instead of closing wave creation.
When Visibility is restricted, every active Drop, Vote, Chat, and Admins group member must also belong to the Visibility group; incompatible rows are highlighted and block progress.
Wave creation verifies the final access groups again after authentication and before creating a personal group for the Admins scope or the Wave.
New inline groups include the connected creator by default, even when the group otherwise contains only rules; choosing a saved group preserves the saved group's membership instead.
Inline identity groups warn when the connected creator is excluded, because excluding yourself from a view group can prevent you from opening the created wave.
All wave types include Rules; Rank and Approve also include Schedule, Drops, and Voting. Scheduled Rank and Approve include Outcomes, while Perpetual Ranking skips Outcomes.

Schedule keeps Submissions Open, Voting Opens, and applicable first-announcement controls visible under Opening dates. Winner schedule or Wave end reveals secondary controls; Perpetual Ranking has no Schedule optional section.
Drops keeps submission type visible and puts optional controls under Submission requirements.
Rules keeps generated wave rules visible and puts optional Wave guidelines and applicable acceptance rules in a Wave guidelines section.
Voting keeps the power model, scope, required Rep or Memes details, and Approve threshold visible; named Vote limits sections contain negative-vote behavior, time weighting, and Approve hold timing.
Outcomes keeps outcome selection, reward configuration, and Show outcomes visible; Approve waves place the optional maximum winner count under Winner limits.
In Description, individual @ mention suggestions follow the draft wave's Visibility group; private drafts suggest only eligible profiles.
The docs for wave creation live under ops/docs/waves/create; on web, use /waves?create=wave to open create-wave mode.

records.title: Chat waves
facts: Chat waves are conversation-focused waves.
Chat wave creation uses Overview, Groups, Rules, and Description steps.
Use Chat when the wave does not need ranking or approval mechanics.

records.title: Rank waves
facts: Rank waves collect drops and allow participants to vote/rank them according to configured rules.
On the Overview step, rank waves choose between Announce Winners (scheduled winner announcements) and Perpetual Ranking (a continuous leaderboard with no winners and no end date).
Rank wave setup includes Overview, Groups, Schedule, Drops, Rules, Voting, and Description; Announce Winners waves also configure an Outcomes step, which Perpetual Ranking waves skip.
Rank wave rules are visible in the desktop right sidebar and mobile About information path.
Leaderboards, winners, and voting state are part of rank-wave participation; perpetual ranking waves keep a live leaderboard but never announce winners or award outcomes.

records.title: Approve waves
facts: Approve waves use approval-oriented voting rather than a plain chat flow.
Approve wave setup includes Overview, Groups, Schedule, Drops, Rules, Voting, Outcomes, and Description.
Approve wave rules are visible in the desktop right sidebar and mobile About information path.
Use Approve when the wave is intended to accept or reject submissions.

records.title: Wave About sections
facts: Desktop wave information sections live in the right sidebar in this order: About, REP, and Configuration.

Configuration is the consolidated rules and settings surface. It includes wave type, access, chat, display, schedules and other generated rules, guidelines, acceptance-required rules, admin-only shared controls, and personal display controls. Approve waves place Approve after, Hold time, Max approved drops, and Approval window directly after Schedule. Shared edits use gears, while read-only creation-time values have no edit control.
For Rank and Approve waves, the desktop right sidebar adds Voters and Activity after the three base sections; Activity moves into More at the fixed panel width.
In the native app, the main About view opens compact Overview, REP, and Configuration pills; Rank and Approve waves expose Voters and Activity from More.
While native About is active, its information pills replace the subwave pills in the same contextual row; selecting another main tab restores the subwave pills.
Selecting a section switches information for the active wave without navigating away from the thread.

records.title: Delete your chat history from a wave
aliases: remove all my wave chat posts
facts: Authenticated profiles can use Delete all my messages from this wave in About -> Configuration.
The destructive button appears between Curations and Your display for connected profiles that are not acting through a proxy.
The action permanently deletes only CHAT drops authored by the current profile in the selected wave.
Submission and winner drops are never deleted by this action.
If the current profile authored the wave's pinned drop, that pinned drop is preserved.
The control remains available if chat was later disabled, so existing history can still be removed.
A confirmation dialog explains the scope and warns that the deletion is irreversible before the API is called.

records.title: Wave rules
facts: All wave creation includes a Rules step. Chat enters Rules after Groups and then goes to Description; Rank and Approve enter Rules after Drops and then go to Voting.
Generated rules summarize the wave setup. Chat rules focus on wave type, access, and chat settings; Rank and Approve rules also include timing, submissions, voting, approval, and outcome visibility.
Creators can add Wave guidelines that are saved as wave metadata and shown under Guidelines in the wave rules panel.

When a wave has guidelines, a profile with no prior chat messages or participation drops in that wave reviews them before its first chat message is sent. Agree sends the pending message; Decline keeps the draft and shows the guidelines again on the next attempt.
For Rank and Approve waves, creators can add rules that require acceptance; those use the existing participation terms and wallet-signature submit flow.
Wave admins can edit Wave guidelines later from Configuration. For Rank and Approve waves, admins can also edit acceptance-required rules there.
Participants can review rules in Configuration in the desktop wave right sidebar or from the mobile About information path.

records.title: Direct message waves
facts: Direct-message waves live under /messages and individual message threads use /messages/{waveId}.
A direct-message creation flow is available at /messages/create.
Direct-message recipient search ranks exact, prefix, and substring handle matches before ENS or auto-wallet matches, then orders each match group from highest to lowest profile level.
Direct messages use wave mechanics but are surfaced separately from standard public wave routes.
Direct-message content stays gated until wallet and profile prerequisites are resolved.

records.title: Wave composer
facts: The wave composer is where users post drops and replies inside a wave.
If a wave has guidelines and the profile has posted neither a chat message nor a participation drop there, submitting its first chat message opens a Wave guidelines dialog before the message is sent.

Agree sends the pending first message and prevents repeat prompts in that wave. Decline or dismissing the dialog does not send the message, keeps the draft, and shows the guidelines again on the next submit attempt.
Composer docs cover markdown, mentions, NFT hashtag references, curation URLs, media uploads, and Enter-key behavior.
On narrow composer rows, the plus button opens a labeled action tray below the input for available Upload, GIF, Poll, Storm, and Metadata actions.

Poll posts require a question, at least two unique options, and a future closing time. The composer explains whether voters can select one option or multiple options and keeps Post unavailable until the poll is valid.

Poll and Storm are mutually exclusive on narrow composer rows: while Poll is open, the plus control and separate Poll action are hidden and the poll header close control removes the poll; while Storm is active, Poll remains visible but unavailable until the Storm is finished or discarded.
On mobile and in the app, the GIF picker uses the same drag handle and swipe-down dismissal as the emoji picker.
Composer availability depends on the wave, groups, permissions, and current state.
If an authenticated wallet has no profile handle yet, public wave content can stay readable while the composer prompts the user to create a profile before participating.

records.title: Manage a post's Curations
facts: Use Add to {Curation name} from a standard post's desktop action menu or mobile touch action sheet to add the post immediately when there is one clear preferred Curation.
While viewing a Curation tab, use Remove from {Curation name} in the same desktop action menu or mobile touch action sheet to remove the post from that active Curation.
Curation-tab posts expose Open drop actions on compact touch layouts, so the mobile action sheet does not require long-press discovery.
Use Manage Curations to choose from every manageable Curation in the source Wave, remove existing membership, or create another Curation.
The dialog lists named Curations in the source Wave that the current account is allowed to manage, with existing memberships first.
Add and Remove update only Curation membership and keep the dialog open; removing a post does not delete its original Wave post.
Create new Curation is separated below the list. Creating from a post adds that post and keeps the user on the current page.
If there is no manageable Curation, eligible users can create the first one and continue adding the same post.
If Curation creation succeeds but adding the post fails, the created Curation remains and the dialog reports the partial success.

records.title: Wave reactions and voting
facts: Drop actions include reactions, ratings, voting, boosting, curation, replies, link copy, and pinning where allowed.
Posted full drops can support emoji reactions and clap rating with optimistic UI and rollback on failure.
Reaction controls are disabled while a proxy profile is active.
Reaction controls are disabled only when chatting and reacting are disabled for the entire wave. A viewer who can see the wave may still react when the wave's chat group does not permit them to post.

If the API rejects the current session, the app starts one authentication recovery attempt for that session and temporarily disables reaction actions. The failed reaction is not automatically replayed.
If a reaction request times out, the app rolls back the optimistic state, refreshes the canonical drop state, and does not automatically retry the write.
Rating controls clamp values to the drop's allowed min/max range and can be disabled when the viewer has no available credit.
Rank/Approve waves expose voting controls such as vote sliders and vote summaries when the user is eligible.
The normal vote dialog can optionally post a standard drop reply with a generated vote rationale prefix; Vote with reply starts off and can be enabled directly or by editing the prefilled text.
When Vote with reply is enabled, removing all rationale text blocks submission until text is added or the switch is turned off.
If an optional rationale reply fails after a successful vote, the vote stays saved and the user is told that the reply failed.
Boosting is a per-user flame toggle on full drop cards and boosted cards in wave and direct-message threads.
Wave creator badges and drop state indicators explain context around submitted drops.

records.title: Wave competition participant and winner badges
facts: A circular violet flag beside a drop author means that author has an active participatory entry in the current wave.
A circular emerald medal beside a drop author means that author has a winning entry in the current wave.
Competition badges can appear on chat, participatory, and winner drops and are scoped to the current wave.
Competition badges do not appear in other waves unless the author also qualifies there.
The wave competition badges are hidden in The Memes Main Stage, which keeps its existing artist badges.
Selecting either badge loads and opens that author's full entries for the current wave; users can switch active and winning sections when both exist.
The entry viewer offers voting only for participatory entries while voting is open, and normal voting eligibility and credit rules still apply.

records.title: Wave slow mode
facts: Wave chat config can set slow_mode_cooldown_ms.
The Wave settings UI shows Slow mode as On with a formatted interval or Off.
When slow mode is active, the composer can show messages like `Slow mode: send again in ...` or `Slow mode: one message every ...`.
Slow mode must be at least 1 second when enabled.

records.title: Edit wave access groups from Configuration
facts: Selecting an access-row gear in Wave Configuration opens the group editor directly without an intermediate context menu.

The Configuration modal renders the same group assignment editor as wave creation, including Edit criteria and Choose group, the privacy row, criteria chips, expanded editors, draft summary, and save actions. It preloads the row's rules, included and excluded identities, NFT and grant requirements, and criteria/member privacy setting.
A public access row starts a new criteria draft with the editor's primary wallet explicitly included by default; Include me can be turned off from Identities.
An already restricted row keeps its saved included and excluded identities and does not add the editor automatically.
Saving edited criteria creates a separate group and normally updates only the selected access row; it does not mutate the original group or other access rows that use it.
When Visibility, Drop, Vote, and Chat access are all public, assigning a Visibility group assigns that same group to all four non-admin access rows in one save and leaves Admins unchanged.
The Visibility cascade does not run when any non-admin access row is already restricted; in that case only Visibility changes and normal containment validation applies.
Visibility offers Make wave public when it is restricted, with a confirmation explaining that everyone will be able to find and view the wave.
Drop, Vote, and Chat access offer Use visibility criteria when their effective criteria differ from Visibility; if Visibility is public, the selected access row becomes public after confirmation.
Admins never offers the Use visibility criteria shortcut.
If the existing criteria or identity lists cannot be loaded, the editor shows a retry state instead of substituting empty criteria.

records.title: Wave chat status settings
facts: Wave chat has two separate settings for Rank and Approve waves: chat.enabled controls whether chat is on, and chat.scope controls who can chat when chat is enabled.
Chat waves require chat to stay enabled, so Configuration does not show a Chat status enable/disable row for them.
Rank and Approve wave Configuration shows Chat status as Enabled or Disabled, and wave admins can edit that row with a gear to enable or disable chat.
The Access row uses Chat access wording; `Anyone` means no chat access group is attached, independently of whether chat is enabled.
Rank and Approve Configuration shows Chat status separately from Chat access, so disabled chat does not look like the same thing as an unrestricted chat access group.

Access groups available to the current viewer—including authorized private groups and direct-message groups for their eligible authenticated members or creators—link from Configuration to a filtered Network view that shows both the group criteria and current members; Configuration displays a live eligible-member count instead of the generated group name.
Use the Clear selected group button in Network to close the group summary and return to the default member view.
A scoped group hidden from the current viewer is labeled `Private group` without a link, name, id, author, criteria, or membership details.
Network does not reuse a selected group's cached criteria or members after the authenticated viewer changes, or while opening a different group.
When chat is disabled, slow mode and disable-links settings are hidden because they only apply when chat is enabled.

records.title: Boosted drops display preference
facts: Wave chat can insert boosted-drop promo cards between normal chronological drops.
The Boosted drops display preference is local to the current device/browser and can be set to Expanded, Compact, or Hidden.
Expanded shows the full inserted boosted-drop card, Compact shows a slim row, and Hidden removes only inserted boosted-drop cards.
Hidden does not hide normal chronological drops that happen to have boosts.
On desktop the control is in the wave right sidebar Settings under Your display; on compact/mobile it is available from the wave header overflow menu.

records.title: Wave leaderboard
facts: Wave leaderboard docs cover winners, my votes, top voters, sales, sorting, price filters, decision timelines, and drop eligibility states.
Leaderboard availability depends on the wave type and configuration.
Use the right sidebar or wave-specific navigation to inspect leaderboard surfaces when available.

records.title: Memes wave submissions
aliases: submit to the memes main stage
can't submit to memes main stage
facts: Memes wave docs cover submission, preview/submit states, additional info fields, and quick voting.
The Memes - Main Stage is a Memes wave context, not the /the-memes collection browse or mint route.
Submission availability depends on login, proxy mode, participation eligibility, the submission window, and per-user submission limits.

If the submit control is hidden or shows a restriction icon or label, select or focus the restriction control to read why submission is unavailable, then recover by logging in, disabling proxy mode, waiting for the submission window, or freeing submission capacity.

In the Artwork step, Continue remains available before required fields are complete, except while an interactive artwork hash is being verified; selecting Continue turns every missing or invalid field and the missing media control red, shows inline recovery messages, and focuses the first missing item in form order.

On larger viewports the artwork remains visible while the metadata form scrolls independently. On smaller viewports the complete form scrolls as one page, focused text fields move into view when the software keyboard opens, and the native modal shrinks to keep its action bar above the keyboard.

On The Memes Main Stage, the desktop How to Submit control and native app lock both open Unlock submissions with the current 50,000 MemesNominee REP requirement, live progress, and a Get nominated action.
Use the wave composer and Memes-specific submission surfaces when participating in Memes waves.

records.title: Groups
facts: Groups are reusable community/member sets used across app workflows such as waves.
On Network, open Filter and then Choose group to search for and apply a saved group.
Criteria-based groups are created inline from workflows such as Network filtering and Wave setup; there is no standalone Network Groups page.
A profile's Groups tab remains available at /{user}/groups.

records.title: Create groups inline
facts: Inline group creators define group details and membership rules inside the workflow where the group is needed.
For selected internal NFTs such as Memes, Meme Lab, Gradients, and NextGen, group creators can require members to own any selected token or all selected tokens.
xTDH grant beneficiary group rules can use typed grant IDs or the grant picker.
For token-specific xTDH grants, group creators can require members to own any specified token or all specified tokens.
For full-collection xTDH grants, group membership requires ownership of at least one collection token.
Group creation requires the relevant connected profile permissions; there is no standalone Network Groups create or edit mode.
Groups can be used later in workflows such as wave access or participation settings.
Include and exclude identity search ranks exact, prefix, and substring profile-handle matches before ENS-only matches, then orders each match group by profile level, highest first.

Across group cards, group details, Wave configuration, member previews, and draft criteria summaries, REP and NIC identity wallets are shown as profile handles when available; identities without a resolvable handle remain visible as wallets.
Publishing a replacement for a group used by a Wave is rejected if it would leave any active Drop, Vote, Chat, or Admins group member outside that Wave's Visibility group.

records.title: Delegation center
facts: Delegation lets one wallet authorize another wallet for supported 6529 uses.
The delegation center provides wallet checking, action flows, collection management, and section navigation.
Delegation is useful for vault/hot-wallet patterns and airdrop-related workflows.

records.title: Wallet Checker
aliases: how can i check my architecture
facts: Wallet Checker lives at /delegation/wallet-checker.
Wallet Checker is a read-only diagnostics page for one wallet.
It checks delegations, delegation managers, and consolidation relationships for an entered Ethereum address or .eth ENS.
It can show Delegations, Active Minting Delegation for The Memes, Delegation Managers, Consolidations, Active Consolidation, and Incomplete Consolidation.
Use Wallet Checker when users ask how to check or view active delegations, consolidations, delegation managers, or wallet-architecture-related setup for an address.

records.title: How to Register a Consolidation
aliases: how do i register a consolidation
how do i set up a consolidation
facts: A consolidation connects wallets you control so 6529 can treat them together for supported metrics such as TDH, total cards, and unique cards; it is consolidation use case #999.
Natural phrases such as adding, linking, pairing, or setting up another wallet refer to this consolidation flow when the goal is for 6529 to treat wallets together for supported metrics.
To register a consolidation, open Register Consolidation from the Delegation Center, choose the collection, enter the Consolidating With address, submit, and execute the transaction.
For TDH consolidation, use Any Collection or The Memes.
Consolidation should be reciprocal when two wallets are intended to be treated together, and it is not a delegation and does not grant rights.

records.title: Register Consolidation Form
facts: The Register Consolidation form is the Delegation Center action for connecting wallets you control for supported 6529 metrics.
The form requires a connected wallet, Collection, and Consolidating With address.
For TDH consolidation, use Any Collection or The Memes.

records.title: Wallet Architecture
facts: The recommended architecture separates a vault wallet for long-term NFT storage, a transaction wallet for trusted marketplace activity, and a minting wallet for unknown or higher-risk minting activity.
The docs call this the Three Address Protocol, or TAP, and explain how separate wallets reduce phishing, malware, and malicious-site risk.
A higher-security version can use SAFE, formerly Gnosis Safe, as the vault wallet, while a more convenient minting wallet can be a hot or mobile wallet.
Use the consolidation docs and Register Consolidation form when you want those wallets treated together for supported 6529 metrics.
For consolidation metrics, 6529 currently recognizes up to 3 addresses as one consolidation group.

records.title: Consolidation Use Cases
aliases: number of wallets in a consolidation
number of addresses in a consolidation
how many wallets can be consolidated
how many addresses can be consolidated
how do i consolidate four wallets
facts: Consolidations help 6529 treat multiple wallets controlled by one collector together for metrics such as total cards, unique cards, TDH, and related collection metrics.
For now, 6529 recognizes up to 3 addresses as one consolidation group for The Memes metrics.
More than 3 addresses can have consolidation records, but Seize only counts the last 3 addresses for consolidation purposes.
Registration capacity and effective counted group size are therefore different: users can create records involving more addresses, while no more than 3 addresses count together.
The docs cover two-address and three-address patterns, plus a four-address compromised-wallet scenario where the user chooses which three-address set should count.
Each address generally needs reciprocal consolidation records with the other addresses it should be grouped with.

records.title: Delegation FAQ
facts: It indexes how-to articles for registering delegations, delegation managers, consolidations, SAFE transaction-builder flows, supported use cases, viewing records, updating, revoking, locking, and unlocking wallets.
Use it when users ask broad Delegation Center how-to questions or ask where the delegation docs live.

records.title: Wallet Connection and Management Clarification
facts: Connecting another wallet to the site is different from consolidating wallets so 6529 treats them together for supported metrics.
Removing or replacing the currently connected wallet is different from changing an on-chain consolidation record.
If the goal is to stop wallets being treated together, open View/Manage in the Delegation Center and revoke the relevant consolidation record.
If the goal is to replace an address on an existing consolidation record, use Update in View/Manage.
If the question is only about the site's currently connected wallet, clarify that it is a connection question rather than a consolidation change.

records.title: How to Revoke a Delegation or Consolidation
aliases: how do i revoke a delegation
facts: To revoke a delegation, delegation manager, or consolidation, open the Delegation Center and choose View/Manage for the relevant collection.
On the Manage/View Collection page, find the address or record you want to revoke and click Revoke.
Execute the transaction to remove the delegation, manager permission, or consolidation record.

records.title: How to Update a Delegation or Consolidation
aliases: how do i update a delegation
facts: To update a delegation, delegation manager, or consolidation, open View/Manage in the Delegation Center for the relevant collection.
Find the address or record you want to update, click Update, adjust the delegated wallet, expiry, or token scope, then submit.
Execute the transaction to apply the update.

records.title: How to Register a Delegation
facts: To register a delegation, open Delegation Center, choose Register Delegation, choose the collection, enter the delegate wallet, select a use case such as #1 All, choose expiry and token scope, then submit and execute the transaction.
A delegation lets another wallet use NFT utility without moving the NFT from the delegator wallet.

records.title: Delegation Manager
facts: A delegation manager gives a manager wallet permission to maintain delegations and consolidations for another wallet.
The docs describe registering a manager from the vault wallet to a delegated wallet, then using that delegated wallet to register future delegations or consolidations.

records.title: Delegate using SAFE
facts: The docs show using the SAFE Transaction Builder with the NFTDelegation.com contract to register delegation manager rights.
The SAFE flow uses the Any Collection value, no-expiry value, use case 998 for Delegation Management, allTokens true, tokenId 0, then creates and sends the batch transaction.

records.title: Delegation and consolidation mapping tools
facts: The delegation mapping tool helps inspect delegation relationships.
The consolidation mapping tool helps inspect wallet consolidation relationships used by 6529 features.
Use these tools when users ask how to check wallet relationships.

records.title: The Memes subscriptions
facts: The Memes subscriptions are an optional way to mint eligible Meme Cards remotely without being online at mint time, with estimated gas savings of about 80% for one card and up to 98% for ten cards funded by one ETH transfer.
Subscriptions are not a mintpass and do not create extra allowlist access.
The setup path is: connect a wallet, open the profile Subscriptions tab, add a completely non-refundable ETH balance, choose Automatic or Manual mode, and select or skip upcoming eligible cards.
The /about/subscriptions primary action says Connect to Subscribe when a wallet or profile handoff is needed and Manage when the user can continue to their profile subscription settings.
Users manage their subscription mode, balance, airdrop address, top-ups, upcoming drops, and history under their profile Subscriptions tab.
Automatic mode mints eligible cards until the balance is used unless the user opts out; Manual mode only mints cards the user opts into.
Automatic mode does not expire when the balance is insufficient; coverage describes what the current balance funds, not an expiration date for the mode.

Coverage counts consecutive fully funded intended drops from the immediate next intended drop and accounts for mode, eligibility, edition preference, selections, opt-outs, balance, and the published schedule.
Coverage is green at 7 or more funded drops, gives an early plan-a-top-up warning at 4 to 6, shows running low at 2 to 3, and requires action at 0 to 1.
When available, Funded through and Next unfunded identify the Meme card and date; Top up by is shown only for an authoritative backend deadline.
If an eligible card is unavailable, no card is airdropped and the unused balance stays available.
The About Subscriptions overview links to the Subscriptions Report for aggregate subscribed and redeemed subscription counts.

records.title: Subscription eligibility
aliases: why can't i mint with subscriptions
facts: Subscriptions do not create extra eligibility.
A subscription can only mint within the phase and allowlist access the profile would otherwise have.
Phase 0 subscription mints are guaranteed because Phase 0 is underallocated; Phase 1 and Phase 2 mints depend on card availability.
When a phase has more subscription mints than available cards, cards are airdropped in the order subscription payments were received.
Top-ups must be received by 00:00 UTC the day before a Meme Card mint to be eligible for that mint.

records.title: Subscription top-up troubleshooting
aliases: sent eth to the subscription address
sent eth to the subscriptions address
sent eth but balance not showing
sent eth but don't see it
where is my subscription top up
where do i top up subscriptions
facts: Subscription top-ups send ETH to the configured subscriptions address on the configured chain.
The Profile Subscriptions tab shows Subscription balance, a refresh balance control, pending or successful top-up transaction links, and Top Up History.

When coverage supplies them, Recommended restores the healthy funded runway and Minimum for next drop covers the immediate at-risk intended drop using the exact required ETH, including a partial shortfall.

If the wallet transaction is still pending, wait for confirmation; if it is confirmed and the balance or Top Up History still does not update after refreshing, share the transaction hash with the tech team.

records.title: Subscriptions report
facts: The Subscriptions Report shows active, upcoming, and redeemed Meme Card subscription counts.
On a mint day, the Active Drop section compares subscribed counts with airdropped counts and keeps that card out of Upcoming Drops and Past Drops.
Active, Upcoming, and Past rows link to the matching /the-memes/{token_id} card route.
It includes download actions for redeemed subscription count reports.
Its Manage or Connect to Subscribe action uses the same profile-subscriptions navigation and authentication handoff as the About Subscriptions page.

records.title: Open Data hub
facts: The Open Data hub collects downloadable data routes and operational data resources.
Open Data includes network metrics downloads, team downloads, royalties uploads, Rememes uploads, and Meme subscription data.
Use /open-data when users ask where downloadable data lives.

records.title: Network metrics downloads
facts: Network metrics downloads are documented under the Open Data area.
Use these routes when users ask where to download TDH or Network metric data.
The Network UI pages explain the metrics; Open Data is for downloadable data access.

records.title: The Memes
facts: The Memes is the main Meme Card collection area.
Use The Memes routes to browse cards, card pages, distributions, and minting-related surfaces.
Individual Meme Card pages and distribution pages live under The Memes route family.
The Memes collection routes are separate from Memes wave submission surfaces in Waves.

records.title: Meme Card minting
facts: Current and upcoming Meme Card mint information is surfaced from home and The Memes-related pages.
Home uses explicit Main Stage mappings for its submission and Meme-card links and omits those links when a mapping is unavailable.

When an unresolved /the-memes/{id} route is the canonical next Meme and its Main Stage winner is explicitly mapped to that id, it shows the winning artwork panel with Mint Date and subscription awareness above the calendar without waiting for the current mint or homepage mode; other upcoming Meme routes keep the standalone subscription and calendar view.

Home Latest Drop and mapped Next Drop cards always show Your allowance. Before a wallet is connected, the row prompts the user to connect to view it. Once connected, wrapping pills list each nonzero Airdrop or Allowlist count for Phase 0, Phase 1, and Phase 2, plus a Public Airdrop count; Public never shows Allowlist. The row distinguishes unavailable distribution data, an unpublished distribution, and a published distribution with no matching allocation; unavailable data does not mean the allocation is zero, and none of these states promises that an allocation is still mintable.
Meme calendar and meme gas routes provide additional minting context.
Subscription minting is a separate optional mechanism and does not grant extra eligibility.

records.title: Meme Lab
facts: Meme Lab is a collection area separate from The Memes.
Meme Lab has collection, individual card, and distribution routes.
The /about/meme-lab overview explains the experimental CC0 artist contract.
Use /meme-lab when users ask where Meme Lab cards live.

records.title: NextGen
facts: NextGen is the generative collection area for collections, tokens, art, minting, and manager tools.
Collection pages live under /nextgen/collection/{collection}.
Token pages live under /nextgen/token/{token}.

records.title: Pebbles
facts: Pebbles is the first NextGen collection.
Pebbles lives at /nextgen/collection/pebbles.
The Pebbles collection pages include overview, art, trait sets, provenance, mint, and distribution-plan views.

records.title: NextGen manager
facts: NextGen manager/admin tools live under /nextgen/manager.
Manager access depends on role and permissions.
Regular users usually browse NextGen through /nextgen, collection pages, or token pages.

records.title: Drop Forge
facts: Drop Forge is the area for claim/drop workflows from craft to launch.
The hub links to Craft and Launch sections, with list and detail pages for each.
Launch claim pages can include mint stats and subscription airdrop sections when configured.

records.title: Rememes submissions
facts: Rememes submission docs cover add-submission behavior and runtime requirements.

Open Data also documents Rememes uploads.

records.title: 6529bot admin and usage
facts: The API tool docs include 6529bot admin and usage documentation.

records.title: App header context

Header behavior changes with route, viewport, and whether the user is inside an app-like layout.
Mobile-web and native-app page sharing appears next to Search on supported routes and opens the platform system share sheet directly.
Use wave header records for wave-specific controls such as wave sharing or wave picture editing.

records.title: Mobile bottom navigation
facts: Mobile layouts use bottom navigation for Discovery, Waves, Messages, Home, Network, Collections, and Notifications.
The mobile bottom navigation surface is separate from the desktop and app sidebar IA.
Tablet-sized app viewports use a wider dock while phone sizing stays unchanged.
Rotating a phone or tablet keeps bottom navigation visible unless a route, edit state, open drop, or real software keyboard hides it.
In the native app, the new-version refresh prompt stays centered directly above the dock and follows its expanded or compact position.

records.title: Mobile pull-to-refresh
facts: Mobile pull-to-refresh is documented as app-shell behavior.

Use it when users ask how to refresh content on mobile.

records.title: Open mobile app landing
facts: The open-mobile route handles mobile app handoff and landing behavior.
Use /open-mobile when users ask how to open the 6529 app from the web.
Mobile navigation and push notification behavior are documented separately.

records.title: Share modal
facts: Supported desktop-web pages show a persistent sidebar Share icon that opens a page-sharing-only modal.
The desktop-web Share dialog places the Browser or App QR target and QR code on the left of wider layouts, with equal-width labeled actions on the right; narrow layouts stack these sections.
Mobile web and the native app open the platform system share sheet directly from the header Share button; they do not open the 6529 Share dialog.

Desktop web uses the Web Share API for the dialog's More action when the secure context, payload support, and document permissions policy allow it; mobile web invokes the Web Share API directly, and the native app invokes Capacitor sharing directly.
Copy changes to a green Copied state for about 1.5 seconds.

System sharing uses the browser URL at invocation time, including search parameters and the hash; on NextGen token routes it removes the transient profile Collected return context before sharing. Cancellation is silent; desktop runtime unavailability hides More and provides accessible feedback, while direct mobile or native failure shows an error without falling back to Copy.

Desktop web supports page sharing on home, while mobile web and the native app hide it there; all three surfaces hide page sharing on Messages, Notifications, and the Messages query view, while Waves and the Waves query view remain shareable.
When a wave is active in the native app, the general Share page button is hidden and the wave-specific arrow share action remains inside the More menu.
Mobile web and native app sharing use their existing header placement and open the platform system share sheet directly.
The profile menu contains Profile and Connect Device; connection targets never appear in the Share modal.
Wave-specific link sharing also exists in the wave header.
Use share controls when users ask how to copy a route or send someone a page.

records.title: Back button behavior
facts: Back button behavior is documented as shared navigation behavior.

facts: Loading and status indicators are shared UI patterns across the app.

records.title: Notifications feed
facts: The notifications feed lives at /notifications.
A connected wallet without a profile sees the profile setup prompt and can open its profile setup route with Create profile.
It supports a responsive multi-select feed filter, row actions, read state, paging, and navigation to related app content.
The notification filter opens as a bottom sheet in the mobile layout and as an anchored dropdown on wider viewports.
Filter choices apply immediately. The mobile sheet stays open while categories are combined, and All clears category filters.
The notification filter defaults to All and can combine Mentions, Replies, Identity, Reactions, Invites, and Subscriptions.
An authenticated user can open Profile Preferences from the Preferences action in their own profile header.
The Invites filter includes wave-created notifications: standard waves the user can access and direct-message waves started with the user.
Standard wave-created rows can offer Join wave and Follow creator controls; direct-message wave-created rows offer Open DM instead of joining the wave.
The Reactions filter includes voted, reacted, and boosted drop notifications; the Identity filter includes new follows and REP/NIC updates.
The Subscriptions filter includes transition-based coverage alerts with runway, Meme context, authoritative deadline when available, and exact minimum top-up action.

records.title: Profile privacy and notification preferences
aliases: people I follow can DM me
facts: Profile Preferences lets an authenticated profile choose whether Everyone, People I follow, or Nobody can start a new direct-message conversation.
